newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: CLOTHING AND FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY WANTS TARIFF PROTECTION TOO
The textile, clothing and footwear industry has called for the federal government to protect its jobs in the same manner as it has moved to protect car industry jobs.
The Council of the Textile and Fashion Industry says its members employ almost twice as many people as the car industry, but tariff reductions threaten a bleak future.
The industry is expecting a draft report from the Productivity Commission this month to decide the future of clothing and footwear import tariffs after the year 2000.
The council wants tariffs on clothing frozen at 25 per cent for five years from 2000, with the same treatment for footwear tariffs at 15 per cent.
It's also called for a renewal of the Imports Credit Scheme, which encourages exports.
PEARSON SAYS GOVT WASHING ITS HANDS OFF EXTINGUISHMENT
Aboriginal leader Noel Pearson says the Federal Government's ten point Wik plan should be rejected because the government is adopting the role of Pontius Pilot.
Mr Pearson told a Sydney luncheon the plan will see the government washing its hands of extinguishing native title, while the state and territory governments will do so.
He says the Commonwealth will adopt the role of Pontius Pilot, washing its hands of direct extinguishment but funding the extinguishment, with compensation payments.
BANS SPARKED BY FIREBLIGHT SCARE LIFTED
State Agriculture Ministers have agreed, in principle, to lift bans imposed on apples, pears and nursey stock from Victoria and South Australia.
Tasmania has decided to lift the bans immediately.
Other states say they'll allow interstate movement of the fruit, subject to advice from a German laboratory, which is carrying out fireblight tests.
The Victorian Agriculture Minister, Pat McNamara, says field surveys of apple and pear orchards in all states have found no evidence of classic fireblight symptoms.
NZ DEMANDS FUMIGATION
New Zealand says the discovery of a redback spider in a consignment of Australian grapes has reinforced the need for fumigation, but is not the reason for it.
Communications manager for New Zealand's Agriculture Ministry, Debbie Gee, says a change in fumigation requirements was agreed on before the start of the year.
Ms Gee says the discovery of the spider, late in February, merely hastened the new requirements.
She says controversy over the decision was probably sparked by the fire blight issue.
She says other countries, like America, have been complying with the new fumigation requirements for over a year, and without complaint.
BEAZLEY WARNED FRONTBENCH AGAINST TREACHERY
The Federal Opposition leader, Kim Beazley, says he fired a bit of a warning to his frontbench against any "treachery" which could undermine Labor.
Mr Beazley has told Channel Nine's Midday Show an Opposition needs to gain the public's confidence, and needs to present a coherent alternative.
He says he did issue a general warning although he hasn't sought to gag Labor MPs.
Mr Beazley says Labor has become a competitive opposition sooner than he expected.
BELL TO DEFEND CHILD SEX CHARGES
Alleged paedophile, Philip Bell has told a Sydney Court he'll defend the 170 child sex charges laid against him after his return to Australia from South Africa last week.
The former Sydney businessman today appeared in Central Local Court where the Director of Public Prosecutions detailed the amount of paperwork involved in the case.
Crown Prosecutor Mark Tedeschi QC said the police brief of evidence is at least twenty volumes containing more than 400 statements from police and civilians.
Mr Bell's legal aid solicitor told the court his client will defend the charges, which allegedly involve twenty boys between 1977 and 1992.
The 63-year-old made no application for bail, and the case was adjourned for a fortnight.
SOCCER SQUAD NAMED FOR OCEANIA QUALIFIERS
Socceroo coach Terry Venables has named a 26-man squad for the six game Oceania World Cup qualifiers.
The squad includes 12 players based with Australian clubs and 14 who played last season overseas.
The squad is intended to cover not only the four matches against the Solomon Islands and Tahiti over the next two weeks, but also home and away matches against what is likely to be New Zealand.
Terry Venables has sought assistance from soccer's world governing body FIFA to secure the release of forward Mark Viduka, whose Croatian club side has not let him join the World Cup squad.

The goalkeepers are Bosnich, Kalac and Jason Petkovic; defenders Tobin, Ivanovic, Horvat, Popovic, Moore, Hooker, Zelic, Muscat, Lazaridis and Tony Vidmar, midfielders Bingley, Slater, Foster, Enes, Skoko, Tapai and forwards Aurelio Vidmar, Mori, Trimboli, Aloisi, Arnold, Zdrilic and Trajanovski.
